cards.title: Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program

cards.title: Tell HN: I've been paying for a rural Tanzanian's education for 10 years

depth.text: someone **paid for a girl's education** for **ten years**, and she got into a master's program

**Anwarite** was 11 when the writer offered to pay her fees. She later graduated from the University of Dar es Salaam with a degree in Language Studies and was accepted into its Master of Arts in Swahili program; the 18-month master's costs **3,060,000 TSh** (about $1,161). The Tanzania Education Project now supports **five students** from Ibumila with school fees and healthcare.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters praise the personal impact; cautious commenters ask about oversight and donor trust, and one questions the value of a Language Studies degree for the region.

comments.text: I highly recommend donating some amount of your time, expertise, or money to good causes, regardless of your financial situation. Even the smallest amounts compound to amazing results—especially over long stretches over time. When I was a student I made (very!) modest contributions to clean water projects, microfinance organizations, and the reports I now read as a mature adult are so gratifying…

I will echo what others have said and say this is amazing on a personal level, but also super cool to share with others. I think especially in tech we can get a little focused on efficacy and scale instead of human impact, and some might quibble about that in the comments ill be interested to see the discourse. Your impact is undeniable, and i think quite importantly very tangible and concrete to…

This is great man. I've been on the other end of this. My annual high school fees cost $700. Couldn't afford it, and it was extremely stressful. If not for the benevolence of my high school principal, I have dropped out. It completely changed my life. You're making a massive difference.

cards.title: Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB

depth.text: someone built **speech-to-text** that runs **on-device**, so your audio stays there

Whistle is a **16.9 MB** model that runs on a CPU with no dependencies. It transcribes English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch and Polish, and can return **word timestamps** or **speech embeddings**.
data: time to first token on 10-second audio

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters praise its accuracy; others report transcription mistakes or say live output is missing.

comments.text: Interesting that this is here. I used whistle (and bunch of other things) to take ownership of my echo show. It now doesn't dial to Amazon at all - it does all processing locally with its own CPU and connects to my homeassistant for home automation. My initial setup involved qwen asr (1.7b model) running on rtx 5080. Compared to that, whistle was really bad (out of 170 messages, qwen recognized…

I don't think the challenge with speech to text was size of the binary. In my experience the challenge is understanding my 84 year old Croatian father with a sagging mouth after a stroke, when he's trying to write his autobiography. I just setup Windows speech to text for him last week and it's great to see how he can write an entire page in 10 minutes, it would take him days using the keyboard…
What the demo does not do is show streaming output of transcribed text as we are speaking and recording (before we hit stop). That is an essential feature IMO for most general purpose live STT apps.

How does this compare with Parakeet? I've been using that locally in my projects on an M-series macbook and it's been working great. It's fast and accurate enough for my use cases (meeting transcription, audio transcription for demo videos, etc.) This definitely seems lighter and faster. How does accuracy compare?

cards.title: 4-hour battery storage is cheaper to install than gas turbines all across globe

depth.text: **four-hour batteries** now cost less than **gas peaker plants** across every market studied

Wood Mackenzie’s comparison uses **levelized cost of electricity** across 43 markets where both technologies were modeled. In the Middle East and Africa, **four-hour storage** is forecast to fall from $120/MWh in 2026 to **$80/MWh by 2035**, a 33% drop that would put it below gas peaking in every gas market there.
data: markets where both technologies were modeled
storage cost in Middle East and Africa, 2026
storage cost in Middle East and Africa, 2035 forecast

cards.camps: Two camps: some see falling battery costs as a turning point for gas peakers; others doubt the forecasts and say four hours won't cover long cloudy, windless spells.

comments.text: I’d like to take a moment to praise the writing here. Rigorous, dense, and well-organized; communicative rather than coughing up tables of raw figures in prose form. I’d refer to the source studies, but at $9,990 per region… Ms Pickerel’s overview seems plenty informative for me. Regarding EMEA: > Grid-scale battery storage costs are now decisively cheaper than gas peaking across the region. [and…

Neither of these assumptions are based on anything other than "That's the number we had to put in to the model to get the conclusion we want".

But, it’s quite abundant on Earth, maybe 3x as abundant as Uranium on earths crust. Because of this abundance it is, along with Radon, the primary constituent of earths natural background radiation.
> No one had ever made the necessary type of laser with a frequency as high as 148 nanometers. No one had ever made the Kessel Run in under 12 parsecs until Han Solo, either.

cards.title: Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature 2026

cards.title: California closed the Montana license plate loophole

depth.text: California changed the law to make the **Montana plate loophole** harder for **shell companies** to use

State Bill 1406 became law on **Sept. 30, 2026**. A shell company counts as a **California resident** if any shareholder, partner, member, or beneficial owner is one. Its officers, managers, partners, beneficial owners, and members can be **personally liable** for unpaid taxes, interest, and penalties.

cards.title: What is Codemode

In Pi, Codemode runs JavaScript in QuickJS inside a WASM runtime on the harness side, separate from the environment that runs bash; it has **no network or file system** and limited RAM. depth.text: someone built a **walkable 3D museum** where you can explore art from **Wikipedia**
It pulls images directly from **Wikipedia's servers**, which one commenter worries could be bad for **Wikipedia's bandwidth**. Another says it is missing **many artists and art movements**.

comments.text: This is incredibly cool. It's been a while since I felt this inspired by something on HN. Congratulations on the idea and the implementation! I genuinely think there's an opportunity for someone (yourself, or someone else) to turn this into a genuinely social experience, a modern museum platform. I'd love to see people's avatars walking around in some suitably tasteful way, with general info on…

This looks incredibly cool! But I do note that it's pulling the images from Wikipedia's servers directly. That feels like it could be pretty bad for Wikipedia's bandwidth. I think I'd feel more comfortable if the art was cached by artfrompixels.com itself, where licensing allows. (And I imagine that for a lot of it there'll be no issue.)

This is super cool and I look forward to sharing with my art friends. One piece of unsolicited feedback: it is really nice to focus on a particular image in the gallery, but when I'm done, it puts me back in normal cursor mode and I have to click to 'step inside' again. Minor annoyance. Otherwise really neat.

What is strange is that last year I spent a lot of time creating the exact same 3D gallery experience with Claude. I picked up the style of the lights, the benches, the walls, the cards position. I also added music, lights on top of the images and the exact tour experience. A year later, I see a very similar implementation!...I find that very odd. But I do like the experience and site, there are…

This is an awesome project. It could bring the art museum experience to those that can't travel to museums. But it is missing so many artists and art movements. A better choice of source material and way more artists can be found on wikiart.org [0]. Maybe the creator could merge scraping efforts? [0] wikiart.org.

glossary.H1B: A US work visa that lets employers hire some workers from abroad for specialized jobs.
glossary.green card: A card showing someone is allowed to live and work in the US permanently.
glossary.501(c)(3): A US legal status for a charitable organization that can let donors deduct donations from their taxes.
glossary.postdoc: A research job someone takes after earning a PhD.
glossary.PhD: Doctor of Philosophy: a degree people work toward by doing original research after earlier university study.
glossary.DAF: Donor Advised Fund: an account people use to set aside money and send donations to charities.
glossary.EIN: Employer Identification Number: a number the US government uses to identify an organization for tax paperwork.
glossary.NGO: Nongovernmental organization: a group that works on a public cause independently of the government.
glossary.CPU: Central Processing Unit: the main chip that runs instructions in a computer.
glossary.word timestamps: Times attached to each word showing when it starts and ends in the recording.
glossary.speech embedding: A bundle of numbers that represents audio in a form software can use without turning it into written words.
glossary.word error rate: A way to score a transcript by how many words it gets wrong; lower means fewer mistakes.
glossary.annualized revenue: An estimate of what a company's revenue would be for a full year if it kept earning at the same pace.
glossary.gross revenue: The total money a company brings in before subtracting its costs.
glossary.cloud partner: A company that helps another business deliver or sell its service through online services.
glossary.three.js: A tool for building animated 3D graphics in a web page.
glossary.subagents: Smaller AI helpers given separate parts of a task to work on at the same time.
glossary.API tokens: Units of text an AI service processes; services can charge based on how many are used.
glossary.KV cache: A store of earlier model calculations that it can reuse instead of doing them again.
glossary.frontier model: One of the most capable, newest AI models available.
glossary.self-hosting: Running a model on computers you control instead of using someone else's online service.
glossary.distilled model: A smaller AI trained to imitate a larger one, so it can be cheaper or easier to run.
glossary.AP: Access point: the part of a Wi-Fi setup that lets devices connect wirelessly.
glossary.IoT: Internet of Things: everyday devices connected to the internet so they can share information or be controlled remotely.
glossary.VLAN: Virtual local area network: a way to split devices into groups on one network so they can’t all reach each other.
glossary.Home Assistant: Software for bringing smart-home controls, like lights and thermostats, together in one place.
glossary.layers: Separate pieces of an image, so one part can be moved or animated without changing the others.
glossary.GUI: Graphical user interface: the buttons, pictures, and menus you use on a screen instead of typing commands.
glossary.lidar: A way to measure the shape of the ground by sending out laser light and measuring what bounces back.
glossary.eink: Electronic ink: a screen that looks more like printed paper than a regular bright screen.
glossary.AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems designed to do tasks people associate with thinking.
glossary.prototype: An early, rough version made to try out an idea.
glossary.metadata: Information describing stored data, like table names or row counts, rather than the records themselves.
glossary.open-source: Software whose code is shared publicly so people can inspect it, change it, or build on it.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.XUL: XML User Interface Language: a language used to change how Firefox looks and works.
glossary.subpictures: Small images used for DVD subtitles and to show which menu choice is selected.
glossary.diegetic menus: Menus presented as part of the film’s world, rather than as a separate screen.
glossary.letterboxing: Showing a wide picture on a narrower screen by adding empty bars above and below.
glossary.pan and scan: Filling a squarer screen by cutting off the sides of a wide picture.
glossary.DVD VM: DVD Virtual Machine: the basic system that handles what happens when you press buttons in a DVD menu.
glossary.safe area: The part of the screen where designers kept important details so they would stay visible on different screen shapes.
glossary.easter egg: A hidden joke or surprise tucked into a game or website.
glossary.Lean: A computer program used to write mathematical proofs and check that their steps are correct.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.Lean certificate: A proof written in a format a computer can check step by step.
glossary.API key: A secret code that lets software use an online service as an approved user.
glossary.point cloud: A 3D shape represented by lots of measured dots.
glossary.content marketing: Promotional material made to attract people to a company or its event.
glossary.LCOE: Levelized cost of electricity: a way to compare the cost of electricity from different power sources over their lifetimes.
glossary.open-cycle gas turbine: A gas power plant that can start quickly for short bursts, but uses fuel less efficiently than plants meant for steady use.
glossary.dunkelflaute: A stretch of winter weather with little wind and sunlight, when renewable power drops.
glossary.nameplate capacity: The maximum power a generator or battery is labeled as able to produce.
glossary.firm capacity: Power a grid can count on being available when it is needed.
glossary.capex: Capital expenditure: money spent up front on equipment or building something.
glossary.nuclear clock: A clock that keeps time by tracking changes in an atom’s nucleus.
glossary.optical lattice atomic clock: A very precise clock that uses light to measure atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
glossary.EM noise: Electromagnetic noise: unwanted effects from electric or magnetic fields that can disturb a measurement.
glossary.maintainer: Someone who keeps a software project working and up to date.
glossary.backdoor: A way into a protected device or service that bypasses its normal security.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.bus factor: How many key people would have to become unavailable before a project struggled to keep going.
glossary.oeuvre: A writer’s oeuvre is the full body of work they have made.
glossary.novel in verse: A novel in verse tells a story using poetry instead of ordinary paragraphs.
glossary.philologist: Someone who studies how language and written works have changed over time.
glossary.etymology: The history of where a word came from and how its meaning changed.
glossary.fragmentary form: A style that leaves gaps or pieces unfinished instead of presenting a complete, smooth story.
glossary.shell company: A company that exists mainly on paper, often used to hold assets or make deals.
glossary.beneficial owner: The person who ultimately owns or controls a company, even if another name appears on its paperwork.
glossary.Use Tax: A tax a state may charge when someone uses a product there after buying it elsewhere.
glossary.off-grid: Able to work without being connected to the main electricity network.
glossary.One-Time Pad: A way to encrypt a message with a secret random key as long as the message, which is never reused.
glossary.Uxn: A small computing system built to run programs written for it.
glossary.emulator: A program that imitates another service so you can try your software without using the real one.
glossary.esolang: An experimental programming language, usually made to explore an idea or for fun rather than everyday use.
glossary.double helix: A shape like a twisted ladder, with two strands winding around each other.
glossary.crystallography: A way to work out what tiny structures look like by studying patterns made when X-rays pass through crystals.
glossary.X-ray diffraction: A method for learning a material’s structure by looking at how X-rays spread after hitting it.
glossary.antiparallel: Describes two DNA strands that point in opposite directions.
glossary.genome: The full set of an organism’s genetic instructions.
glossary.methylome: A collection of chemical marks that help control which genes are active.
glossary.low entropy: Here, it describes chemical marks linked to mitochondrial processes that looked unusually unchanged with age.
glossary.mitochondria: Parts inside cells that help them produce energy.
glossary.healthspan: The part of a person’s life spent in good health.
glossary.lathe: A machine that spins a piece of material while a cutting tool shapes it.
glossary.boring mill: A machine that cuts and shapes a hole inside a metal part.
glossary.slide rest: A carriage that holds a cutting tool and moves it along a lathe.
glossary.lead screw: The long screw that moves a lathe's carriage in step with the turning work.
glossary.three-plate method: A way to make a flat surface by scraping and comparing three plates.
glossary.backlash: The lost movement when a screw turns but the part has not started moving yet.
glossary.chatter: Vibration that makes a cutting tool bounce and leave an uneven surface.
glossary.closed-form solution: An exact answer written as a mathematical expression, rather than just a decimal approximation.
glossary.sock puppet: An alternate online account used by the same person, often without making that link clear.
glossary.Base64: A way to represent data as ordinary text characters, even when the data itself is not text.
glossary.STEM: Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics: subjects about how the world works, how to build things, and numbers.
glossary.Oxbridge: A nickname for Oxford and Cambridge universities.
glossary.prefect: A student given authority to help supervise and discipline other students.
glossary.rent-seeking: Making money by controlling something valuable without creating much useful value yourself.
glossary.survivorship bias: Judging success by looking only at the winners and overlooking the people or attempts that didn't make it.
glossary.cancellation argument: A proof step that depends on two quantities or effects canceling each other out.
glossary.formalization: Writing mathematics in a precise form that a computer can check.
glossary.predicate: A check asking whether something is true, with an estimate of how likely that is.
glossary.loop-invariant: A condition whose answer stays the same each time a loop repeats.
glossary.branch-free: Code that runs without choosing between different paths.
glossary.batch: A group of items handled together in one go.
glossary.vectorization: Running one operation over a group of values together instead of one at a time.
glossary.projection: A database step that keeps only selected columns from each row.
glossary.join: A database operation that combines data from multiple tables.
glossary.coproduct: A type that can hold one value from either of two alternatives, like nothing or a walrus.
glossary.guard clause: A check near the start of a function that handles or exits on a special case.
glossary.403 error: A message saying the website understood your request but won't let you in.
glossary.PaaS: Platform as a Service: online tools and a place to build or run software.
glossary.RL: Reinforcement Learning: a way to teach an AI by rewarding actions that get the desired result.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.framerate: How many new pictures a game shows each second, which affects how smoothly it moves.
glossary.prompt compliance: How well an AI follows the instructions you give it.
glossary.Codemode: A way for an AI agent to coordinate tool calls and combine them in code.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.JavaScript: A programming language; here, it lets an agent combine tool calls.
glossary.QuickJS: A program for running JavaScript; Pi uses it to run Codemode code.
glossary.WASM: WebAssembly: a way for an app to run plug-ins written in other programming languages.
glossary.EMP-resistant: Electromagnetic pulse-resistant: designed to keep working despite a burst of energy that can disrupt electronics.
glossary.shoring: Supports added to hold up a tunnel’s walls or ceiling.
glossary.static recompilation: Translating a game's existing code into code for a different system before running it.
glossary.WebAssembly: A way to run compiled programs inside a web browser.
glossary.HLE kernel: High-Level Emulation kernel: a simplified stand-in for the PSP's operating system that handles requests from games.
glossary.WebGL2: A browser feature that lets websites draw interactive 3D scenes.
glossary.JIT: Just-in-time compilation: compiling a program as it runs, rather than beforehand.
glossary.masking tape: Tape used to cover parts you don't want painted, so the paint leaves a clean edge.
glossary.router: A power tool used to smooth or shape the edges of wood.
glossary.treated lumber: Wood treated to help it hold up outdoors.
glossary.exposition: A clear explanation of an idea or result, not just the result itself.
glossary.corollary: A result that follows from something already proved.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change shared so others can review it.
glossary.median: The middle value when the results are put in order.
glossary.recommendation system: A feature that picks which posts or videos to put in front of you next.
glossary.chronological feed: A list of posts shown in the order they were posted.
glossary.echo chamber: A space where you mostly see views like your own, so they keep getting repeated.
glossary.influence campaign: A planned effort to shape what people think by spreading messages.
glossary.IIIF: International Image Interoperability Framework: a shared way for museums to make detailed images available for zooming.
glossary.VR: Virtual reality: a computer-made view that replaces what you see around you.
glossary.cached: Saved as a copy so it can be loaded later without downloading it again.
glossary.provenance: The record of where an artwork came from and who owned it.
